en: The practitioner Śrīpāda Dhyānacandra Gosvāmī, having risen during the *brāhma-muhūrta*, should remember or chant the names of his own chosen deity:
"Victorious is He of pure prowess!"
Golden-hued, with eyes as broad as lotuses, his noble arms reaching down to his knees,
he dances in manifold ways through the aesthetic flavor of devotion.
"Śrī-Rāma," "Janārdana," "Lord of the Worlds," "Nārāyaṇa," "Bliss," "Compassionate One," "Beloved of Kamalā," and "Kṛṣṇa"—
repeatedly submerged in the surging waves of the great ocean of the nectar of these glorious names.
O Lord, always protect me, who am bewildered, whose eyes are filled with falling tears, and who am helpless.
"Śrī-kānta, Kṛṣṇa, Karuṇāmaya, Kañjanābha, Kaivalya-vallabha, Mukunda, Murāntaka"—
this series of names is like a necklace of pure pearls for the Goddess Lakṣmī.
I shall place around my neck that which steals away all beauty.
O Kṛṣṇa, Rāma, Mukunda, Vāmana, Vāsudeva, Teacher of the World!
O Matsya, Kūrma, Narasiṃha, Varāha, Rāghava, protect me!
O Ocean of Compassion, worshipped by the lords of gods, dānavas, Nārada, and other great sages!
O son of Devakī, grant me unwavering devotion to Your feet.

O Gopālaka, O ocean of the waters of mercy, O Lord of the daughter of the ocean, O slayer of Kaṃsa, O You who have crossed to the further shore of compassion for the lordly elephant, O Mādhava! O younger brother of Rāma, O teacher of the three worlds, O lotus-eyed One, [protect] me!
O Lord of the gopīs, protect me; I know no one other than you.
O Śrī Nārāyaṇa, lotus-eyed one; O Śrī Rāma, Lord of Sītā; O Govinda, Acyuta, son of Nanda; O Mukunda, Ānanda, Dāmodara;
O Viṣṇu, Rāghava, Vāsudeva, Nṛhari, crest-jewel of the lords of gods!
O Hari, O Śrī Kṛṣṇa, helmsman of the ocean of saṃsāra, obeisances unto You!
O Bhāṇḍīra tree, O ornament of the peacock-feather crown, O you whose limbs are anointed with sandalwood paste, O Indra of the Vṛndāvana forest, O dark one with shimmering, large blue lotuses,
O beloved of the Yamunā, O son of Nanda, O you whose eyes are like the lotus of supreme bliss!
O Śrī Govinda, O Mukunda of beautiful form, gladden me, who am wretched! GGS_7 //
O Goddess whose girdle is the ocean, whose breasts are the mountains, O Consort of Viṣṇu, salutations to you; forgive my touching your feet. (GGS 8)
Then, having gone outside, one should perform the ritual procedures such as the practice of loving-kindness (*maitrī*),
attend to the cleansing of the teeth and other such acts,
and sit upon a pure seat facing the east with a steady mind.
One should remember the glorious Gauracandra on the southern bank of the celestial river,
within the heart-abode that is like a wish-fulfilling gem, known as Śrī Navadvīpa.
On the beautiful bank of the celestial river, there shines a place whose body resembles the back of a vast tortoise;

it is surrounded by lovely groves and encircled by clusters of great palaces made of fine jewels and gold, where the dance of Kṛṣṇa’s congregational chanting— resplendent with the weight of overflowing love— is performed eternally before every temple.
I praise Śrī Navadvīpa, which is non-different from the forest of Vṛndāvana and is peerless throughout the three worlds.
The banks of which shine with the excellence of blossoming, glorious trees and creepers; which is beautiful with rows of waves;

where swarms of bees find their abode amidst gentle breezes, flocks of swans, and clusters of lotuses; and which possesses a multitude of divine bathing places (tīrthas) strewn with excellent jewels—[this is] the Śrī-Gaura-pādāmbuja [lake].
The purifying Gaṅgā exists, her body covered and grey with dust.
In the midst of its beautiful golden rivers, the great and auspicious Śrī Navadvīpa shines forth, a source of joy for the enemy of Madhu;
it is delightful with various trees and creepers rich in flowers and fruits, and is frequented by the great.
For it captivates the heart and the ears with the warbling of flocks of birds of various colors.
Its trunk is of emerald; its many branches are of gold; its rows of leaves are as delicate as rubies; its buds are made of coral;
its mass of flowers consists of excellent diamonds; and its fruit is of lapis lazuli.
There is some particular cluster of trees belonging to him, in which [the fruit] is exceedingly brilliant.
In its center is a courtyard delightful with rows of houses for the assembly of noble twice-born beings, a place of pleasure-pavilions upon altars shining amidst rows of gardens and groves,
where there is an eternal festival of great devotees resplendent with the splendor of true devotion.
In this city, there shines a great image of Aghāri in every house.

Having thus established residence in the mind within the center of Śrī Navadvīpa, one should perform service there for the venerable Guru-deva in the proper sequence, beginning with his rising from bed, washing his face, and brushing his teeth. After the service, one should meditate as it is stated in the Yāmala—
therein is the meditation on the venerable Guru:
The eternal Śiva, whose lotus feet are filled with the nectar of compassion, who is clad in white garments, possesses a fair complexion,
and is the abode of all virtues, adorned with beautiful garlands and ornaments.
I remember my guru, who is truly devoted to Hari.
Following the lineage of one's own guru, the parama-guru, the parātpara-guru, and the parameṣṭhi-guru, one should go to the temple of Śrīman Mahāprabhu.
There, by His command, one should perform service for the Moon of Navadvīpa, beginning with the ritual of rising from bed and the washing of the lotus-face with fragrant water.
Regarding the meditation on Śrīman Mahāprabhu there, it is as stated in the Ūrddhvāmnāya (3.15):
Two-armed, with a complexion as radiant as gold, his hands displaying the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness,
he is joined in a loving embrace and chanting the name of Hari.
Immediately thereafter, one should meditate upon Śrī Vṛndāvana:
"Vṛndāvana is surrounded by divine creepers,
and the creepers possess tips shimmering with blossoming flowers."
Even the flowers are filled with abundant bees,
and the bees sing songs that steal the ear.
In the midst of beautiful Vṛndāvana, adorned with fifty groves,
within a bower of desire-trees, there is a house made of divine jewels.

There, with a perfected body, one should remember the nocturnal pastimes of Śrī Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa as follows: At the end of the night, although Śrī Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa have been awakened by the recitation of verses from the multitude of extremely clever parrots and starlings appointed by Śrī Vṛndā— who are full of aesthetic mellows— they remain awake for a moment, unable to endure the interruption of the bliss of their deep embrace, and they feel a sense of agitation at the end of the night as those various verses are recited.

Having arisen from their respective flower-couches in the groves, filled with inner bliss by the playful jests of the assembly of dear friends such as the illustrious Lalitā and Viśākhā who had arrived at that time, yet feeling apprehensive upon hearing the harsh words of Jaṭilā, the two of them— unable to bear the fear of separation and agitated by both terror and longing— departed for their respective homes.
In this manner, one should gradually remember the pastimes of Śrī Gauracandra and of Śrī Rādhā-Kṛṣṇa.
After remembering the pastimes of the end of night, one should prostrate like a staff before the guru and others, as follows:
"To me, who am blinded by the darkness of ignorance, with the collyrium-stick of knowledge..."
Salutations to that venerable guru by whom the eye has been opened.

Having recited this mantra and prostrated like a staff before the venerable Guru, one should likewise prostrate like a staff in succession before the Supreme Guru, the Guru beyond the supreme, the Preceptor (Parameṣṭhi), and the Gosvāmī’s feet;
thereafter, one should prostrate before Śrī Gauracandra:
"To Viśvambhara, to Gaura, to Caitanya, the Great Soul..."
Salutations again and again to the son of Śacī, to the friend, to the lord of Lakṣmī.
I salute the Eternal Bliss, who has a pearl pendant hanging from his ear,
and who has sanctified the earth in the form of Caitanyāgraja.
To that compassionate one who has delivered all people,
whose mind is submerged in the ocean of the nectar of love,
and who is honored and worshipped by Caitanyacandra; to him [I bow].
I bow my head to Advaitacandra.
O Gadādhara, salutations to you, whose very life is Gaurāṅga;
salutations to you, O Śrī-Śrīnivāsa Paṇḍita, the embodiment of divine love! GGS_23 //
In this manner, one should prostrate like a staff before the assembly of Gaurī’s devotees in due order, saying:
"Obeisance to the abode of Śrī Navadvīpa; obeisance to Śrī Gaṅgā."
Salutations to Śrī Saṅkīrtana!
Salutations to the illustrious Gauḍa Maṇḍala!
To him who is more beautiful than ten million Cupids and possesses the luster of a blooming blue lotus!
Salutations to the son of the Lord of the Gopas, whose divine play enchants the world.
O Rādhā, whose limbs are fair as molten gold, Sovereign Lady of Vṛndāvana,
Daughter of Vṛṣabhānu, Goddess beloved by Hari, I bow down to you!
To her who is as dear to Śrī Rādhikā as Her own life,
who has been taught the excellence of happiness by Viśākhā,
and whose bodily sweetness overflows with the nectar of divine play.
I bow to Mañjarī, who was previously bodiless.
Salutations to the groups of supreme and most beloved friends beginning with Lalitā;
salutations to the groups of friends beginning with Kusumikā;
salutations to the groups of eternal friends beginning with Kastūrī.
Obeisance to the hosts of life-companions, headed by Śaśimukhī; obeisance to the hosts of dear companions, headed by Kuraṅgākṣī;
obeisance to the mañjarīs, headed by Śrī Rūpā.
Obeisances to the multitude of friends headed by Śrīdāmā; obeisances to all the cowherds and cowherd girls;
obeisances to the inhabitants of Vraja.
Obeisances to the forests of Śrī Vṛndāvana! Obeisances to the circle of the Śrī Rāsa dance!
Obeisances to the Śrī Yamunā!
Obeisances to Śrī Rādhā-kuṇḍa and Śyāma-kuṇḍa. Obeisances to Śrī Govardhana. Obeisances to the twelve sacred forests.
Obeisances to the sacred district of Vraja.
Obeisances to the sacred district of Mathurā.
Obeisances to all the incarnations.
Salutations to the infinite hosts of Vaiṣṇavas;
salutations again and again to those who are wish-fulfilling trees, oceans of compassion, and the purifiers of the fallen. GGS 27.
Then one should perform the bath as follows: facing the current in a river and so forth, or facing east in a pond or similar body of water, one should invoke the sacred fords (tīrthas) as follows:
"O Gaṅgā, Yamunā, Godāvarī, Sarasvatī, Narmadā, Sindhu, and Kāverī—be present in these waters! (GGS 28).

O compassionate Gaṅgā, who destroys great sins; O you who shine upon the supreme head of Maheśa; O you whose heart is a stage for splendor; O you born from the lotus feet of Acyuta, the abode of flowing Brahman—protect me!
Purify us, O maiden, you who are blessed with the waves of your current!
From the midst of the water at Viṣṇu’s navel, an excellent lotus arose; from its stalk, which was Mount Sumeru, you, O Blessed One, were born as a flowing stream from the world of Brahmā.
Having fallen from the sky onto the head of Rudra, whose hair was bowed down by your waters, you went to the earth—thus you are Gaṅgā.
Who is it that would not salute you, who have been purified by contact with Madhumathana, Hara, and Brahmā?
Whoever should utter "Gaṅgā, Gaṅgā," even from a distance of hundreds of yojanas,
is liberated from all sins and goes to the world of Viṣṇu.
She is the eternal recipient of supreme love from the Sun of Consciousness and Bliss, the son of Nanda; her body is composed of the fluid Brahman;
she is the cutter away of sins and the sustainer of the world’s welfare.
May the daughter of Mitra purify our bodies.
O Rādhikā-kuṇḍa, you who possess fortune equal to Rādhikā’s and are praised by all holy places, be gracious; I bathe in your auspicious waters.
Then, having put on white garments and having performed the wearing of the temple of Śrī Hari, one should mark the limbs with the syllables of Śrī Hari’s name—
one should meditate on Keśava on the forehead, Nārāyaṇa on the belly, Mādhava on the chest, and Govinda in the hollow of the throat. (GGS 34)
One should place Viṣṇu on the right side of the belly, Madhusūdana on the arm,
Trivikrama on the neck, and Vāmana on the left side.
One should place Śrīdhara on the left arm, Hṛṣīkeśa on the neck, Padmanābha on the back, and Dāmodara on the hips;
then, one should apply the water used for washing that [image] to the head with the mantra "Vāsudeva. (GGS 36)

As before, remaining in a steady posture with a steady mind, one should first meditate upon and worship Śrī Śrī Kṛṣṇa Caitanya Deva— who is seated upon a jeweled throne in the Śrī Ratna Mandira in the center of Śrī Navadvīpa, and who is served by a multitude of devotees— following the lineage beginning with the Guru. Therein, one should first meditate upon the temple of Śrī Jagannātha Miśra.
As it is said in the Caitanyārcana-candrikā:
"The courtyard of Śrī Jagannātha Miśra’s temple was a city of variegated mansions, adorned with various jewels and gems by the most excellent [of beings]. (GGS 37)
In its center is the city of the glorious abode of Nārāyaṇa, with a golden rampart that puts the splendor of the sun to shame, featuring a courtyard for congregational chanting shining at the front,
an inner harem for Lakṣmī, kitchens, pleasure gardens, bedchambers, and a magnificent moon-chamber.
That which shines forth from the fair-limbed Hari, bestowing happiness and augmented by his own bliss; // GGS_38 //
In its center is a pinnacle of nine crest-jewels, with precious gems between the turrets; it is adorned with pearl garlands and variegated golden plates,
and is embellished with doorways of the Vedas, beautiful jeweled thresholds, and well-polished gemstone panels.
A palace adorned with real moonlight, lotus-gems, and moonstones.
In its center, upon the lotus of the glorious Yoga-seat (yoga-pīṭha)— which is fashioned of gold inlaid with jewels, endowed with the diagrams of the mantra-syllables,
resembling the beauty of the filaments at the tips of the pericarp within a hexagon,
and possessing the supreme splendor of the Tortoise-shaped Yoga— [The Lord dwells.]
Upon that lion throne, which shines with the stainless brilliance of a million moons and suns, [he sits].

With its sides and base fashioned from lotus-patterned cloth, its pillars of sapphire with backs of lapis lazuli, draped with variegated canopies and hanging strings of excellent gems and great pearls;
with a seat of Chinese silk at its edge of cotton, and a pillow with a surface as soft as the moon.
It has a golden core, its various mantras are variegated, and its eight sheaths are reached through meditation on the feet of the Lord who takes away all wealth.
In the center of that, one should meditate upon Śrī Gauracandra; to His left, Śrī Gadādhara;
to His right, Avadhūtendra; and then Śrī Advaita.
To the south of that, one should meditate upon Śrīnivāsa, the most excellent of wise sages;
and one should meditate upon the multitude of Śrī’s devotees, beautifully surrounding him on all four sides.
One should remember one's own spiritual masters situated among their respective groups within the assembly of the illustrious Gauras' devotees, headed by Rūpa and Svarūpa.

In that regard, first is the remembrance of the venerable Guru, as stated in the *Sanatkumāra-saṃhitā*: "Resembling ten thousand moons, with hands shining with the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, wearing white garments, and adorned with divine white garlands and unguents. (GGS 45)
One should meditate upon him who has a serene face, who is peaceful, who is blissful through the joy of devotion,
who bears a divine form, who grants boons, and whose eyes are like lotuses.
The pure practitioner should meditate with his mind upon a Guru of such a form—one who has followed the assembly of former teachers of form and is eager to serve. GGS 47.
One should contemplate oneself as being eager for service in His presence,
with a neck adorned by the tilaka of the divine and glorious temple of Hari, a chest graced by a beautiful garland,
and further beautified by the letters of the holy name of Hari and anointed with sandalwood paste.
One should meditate upon one's own self as standing near the lotus feet of the venerable Guru, clad in pure, bright new garments, constantly maintaining a stainless body, and eager for service.
His hair is bound with a beautiful string of pearls; his moon-like face is beautifully smiling;

he wears fine garments variegated with sandalwood and aguru paste; he is adorned with divine garlands and ornaments; he is sweet with the joy of relishing the aesthetic flavor of the immersion in dance; and he is radiant in the attire of Kandarpa.
I worship Caitanya, who possesses the luster of gold and is served by his own people.
To Him whose beautiful gait is censured by the lord of lotuses, whose glorious feet are clothed in robes as dark as a row of blue lotuses, who outshines the evening moon with the luster of His body,
and whose smiling face possesses eyes like intoxicated *khañjana* birds in full-blown lotuses trembling with love;
I constantly remember the eternally blissful one, whose bodily splendor is radiant with ornaments.
I bow to Him whose lotus feet are served by the swarm of true devotees, who wears garments as white as jasmine flowers and the moon,
whose complexion has the luster of pure gold, who possesses a pair of beautiful arms, whose face is smiling, who is handsome,
whose eyes are like those of Śrī Caitanya, who grants boons and fearlessness with His hands, and who is adorned with ornaments of divine love.
I constantly remember the Lord, non-dual and the sole root of supreme bliss.
I behold the moon-like Śrī Gauracandra, whose lotus feet are the nectar-essence of pure compassion,
whose right hand is skillful in the gesture of offering betel, who is clad in white garments and is the most excellent of beings;
his body is composed of the bliss of divine love, his face bears a smile like nectar, and he gazes with eyes like the moon.
One should meditate upon Śrī Gadādhara, the best of the twice-born, resplendent with the ornament of sweetness.
They drink the nectar from the lotus feet of Śrī Caitanya; they are radiant with the ornament of true love;
they possess the luster of pure gold; their limbs are graced by tears, horripilation, and perspiration;
with hands bearing offerings for service, they have smiling faces, wear white garments, and are most excellent.
May we meditate upon those great-souled attendants, such as Śrīvāsa and others, who are composed of bliss.

Thus, immediately after this recollection, by the command of the venerable guru, one should worship the illustrious Mahāprabhu with the sixteen types of offerings (*ṣoḍaśopacāra*) and other services using His root-mantra (*mūla-mantra*) alone.
The extraction of the mantra of the illustrious Mahāprabhu is as follows; in the *Ūrdhvāmnāya*, the words of Śrī Nārada to Śrī Vyāsa (3.14–16):
"Oh! You have proclaimed a most profound question."
O Brahmin, I shall declare to you the auspicious mantra that bestows great merit.
"Klīṃ, obeisance to Gaurāṅga"—thus he is worshipped in all the worlds.
Worshipped with the seed-syllables of Māyā, Ramā, and Anaṅga, as well as the seed-syllable of Speech, this six-syllabled king of mantras is celebrated as the celestial wish-fulfilling tree. (GGS 55)
The mantra is as follows: *klīṃ* *gaurāya* *namaḥ*; *hrīṃ*, *śrīṃ*, *klīṃ*.
Aiṃ, salutation to Gaurī.
This is the water for the feet; this is the respectful offering.
This is the water for sipping,
this is the fragrance,
this is the flower.
This is incense, this is a lamp, this is the food offering.
This is drinking water, this is water for sipping,
and this is betel.
"This is the fragrant garland,
this is the handful of flowers," and so forth;
in this manner, one should worship the Lord Śrī Nityānanda.
The extraction of the mantra of the illustrious Lord Nityānanda is as follows (in the *Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa*, in the dialogue between Dharaṇī and Śeṣa):
"Listen to this hundred-name mantra that has been declared;
it was previously taught by me to you under the designation 'Kāma-bīja'. (GGS 56)
With the seed-syllable of fire (RAṂ) at the end of the word *pūta*, preceded by "O God, salutation" (*namaḥ deva*),
and the word *jāhnavī* in that same place, followed by *vallabhāya*— this twelve-syllable mantra is captivating in every respect. (GGS 57)
The mantra is as follows: *kḷiṃ deva-jāhnavī-vallabhāya svāhā*.
One should worship with this very mantra;
in this manner, one should worship the Lord Śrī Advaita.
Now, the extraction of the mantra of the venerable Advaita-prabhu is as follows, according to the *Padma Purāṇa*:
"O Nārada, best of sages, this question is most profound; indeed, you must not reveal this great secret, which is more secret than the secret. (GGS 58)

Joined with the seed-syllable of desire (KĀM), the mistress of the fire of non-duality (VAHNI), and ending with "ṄE," this mantra, consisting of the color of a sage (ṚṢI), is indeed extremely difficult to obtain. // GGS_59 //
The mantra is as follows: *klīṃ advaitāya svāhā*.
Immediately after that, one should worship Śrī Gadādhara Paṇḍita with the remains of the offerings (*nirmālya*) of the venerable Mahāprabhu, using his very mantra.
The mantra of Śrī Gadādhara Paṇḍita is as follows: *śrīṃ gadādharāya svāhā*.

Then, in that same manner, one should worship the devotees such as Śrī Śrīvāsa, as well as the assembly of gurus and others, with the prasāda of Mahāprabhu’s remains; however, one should worship the venerable Guru and the Deity using their respective names in the dative case, while worshipping the Guru specifically with his root mantra (*mūla-mantra*).
Regarding the extraction of the mantra for the venerable Guru, it is as follows in the *Bṛhad-Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa*, in the dialogue between Sūta and Śaunaka:
"Śrīṃ gum"—this is the mantra for the venerable Guru; the ten-syllabled king of mantras, Vahni-vallabhā, is the protector in all undertakings. (GGS 60)
The mantra is as follows: *Śrīṃ guṃ bhagavad-gurave svāhā*.

Then one should take the remaining offerings, such as the *nirmālya*, and having placed them in another location, one should offer a handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*) at the lotus feet of the Lord and perform the *ārātrika* ceremony.

Immediately after that, having performed the waving of the yak-tail fan (*cāmara*) and other rites, while standing beside the venerable Guru, one should perform a visual inspection according to the sequence of meditation and then perform the external worship (*bahiḥ-pūjā*).
Having performed the external worship, one should subsequently recite the respective *gāyatrī* mantras in order.
Among these, first is the *gāyatrī* of the venerable Guru, as stated in the *Padma Purāṇa*: "Śrīṃ! We know the divine Guru; we meditate upon him who is dear to Gaurī; may that Guru inspire us."
First one should perform worship of the mantra-teacher, and afterwards the worship of me;
by doing so, one attains success, for otherwise it would be fruitless.
At the beginning of meditation and so forth, one should contemplate the form of the glorious Guru; at the beginning of worship and so forth, one should perform the worship of the Guru;
and at the beginning of recitation and so forth, one should employ the mantra of the Guru; for otherwise, it shall be fruitless. (GGS 62)
Then, regarding the characteristics of *japa*, as stated [in the Śrī Hari-bhakti-vilāsa 17.143, 129]:
"One should not shake the head or the neck, nor should one show one's teeth. Mental concentration, purity, silence, and reflection on the meaning of the mantra [are required]. (GGS 63)
The mantra is situated in the midst of the mind, and the mind is situated in the midst of the mantra;
when the mind and the mantra are thus perfectly united, this indeed is the defining characteristic of recitation (japa).
Now, the rule regarding the fingers for recitation (*japa*) and so forth (*Śrī Hari-bhakti-vilāsa* 17.116–120):
In that regard, one performing recitation with the fingers should do so using all the fingers including the thumb.
An action performed without the thumb shall be fruitless. (GGS 65)
The little finger, the ring finger, the middle finger, and the fourth [finger] is considered the index finger;
three of these fingers should have three joints, while the middle finger has only one joint.
One should avoid the two joints of the middle finger at the time of recitation;
thus one should know Meru to be defiled by Brahmā himself. (GGS 67)
Starting from the middle of the ring finger and proceeding clockwise in sequence, one should [place them] successively upon the ten joints up to the base of the index finger. (GGS 68)
One should not separate the fingers; one should slightly contract the palm.
For if there is a separation between the fingers, the recitation flows away through the gaps. (GGS 69)
Regarding the statement "the middle finger has one joint," some take this to mean the middle joint of the middle finger; that is not correct.
Now, the sequence for recitation (*japa*) is as follows: first, one should call to mind the *mantra-gāyatrī* of one's Guru and deity.
Then follows the chanting of the Gāyatrī mantra of Śrī-Gauracandra.
One should then recollect the Gāyatrī mantra of non-duality belonging to the venerable Lāvadhūtendra, and then that of the venerable Gadādhara and Śrīvāsa Paṇḍita. (GGS 71)
The mantra of the venerable Guru is as follows: *śrīṃ guṃ bhagavad-gurave svāhā*.
Now, the Gāyatrī: *śrīṃ gurudevāya vidmahe, gaura-priyāya dhīmahi,*
"May that Guru inspire us.
Following this recollection of the Śrī-Guru-Gāyatrī, one should remember the lineage of Gurus;
the sequence of remembrance is as follows:

Having performed meditation according to one's own respective tradition, starting from the Śrī Guru and the Parama Guru and extending up to the Lord of one's own assembly, the Supreme Preceptor (Parama-parameṣṭhi), and the Guru, and having recited their respective names in the dative case, one should thereafter remember the mantra and the Gāyatrī of Śrī Śrī Caitanya Mahāprabhu.
The mantra is as follows: *klīṃ gaurāya svāhā*.
The Gāyatrī is as follows: *klīṃ caitanyāya vidmahe viśvambharāya dhīmahi tan no gauraḥ pracodayāt*.
The mantra is as follows: *klīṃ devajāhnavīvallabhāya svāhā*.

The extraction of the mantra of Śrī Rādhā is as follows, according to the *Gaurī-tantra*: "Combined with the venerable *nāda* and *bindu*, likewise joined with fire (*ra*), the face (*i*), and the circle (*u*), followed by the fourth [case-ending] and the wife of fire (*svāhā*)—this is the eight-syllabled mantra of Rādhikā. (GGS 181)
The mantra is as follows: *śrīṃ rāṃ rādhikāyai svāhā*.
The Gāyatrī is as follows: *śrī-rādhikāyai vidmahe, prema-rūpāyai dhīmahi*.
May that Rādhā inspire us.
Her meditation is described in that very same place:
"She is smiling, possessing the luster of beautiful saffron, with her face veiled by the fluttering edge of a garment of shimmering crimson."

I worship Rādhikā, who is sweet throughout the three worlds; she is beautiful with her attire, with a lotus hanging from the locks of hair tied in a braid, and with long eyes reaching to her ears; she holds a betel leaf in her hand and applies it to Hari’s lotus-like face by joining her forefinger and thumb. GGS_182 //
She has the luster of molten gold, with jasmine flowers bound in her dark tresses;
her face is like the autumn moon, and her eyes are as flickering as a cakorī bird in flight.
She possesses the moonlight of a smile upon her bimba-fruit lips, which bestows life upon the world,
and is adorned with a pearl necklace hanging from her beautiful jeweled breasts.
She wears a blue garment upon her hips, is adorned with a network of tinkling bells,
and wears jeweled anklets fashioned from various gems and precious materials.

I take refuge in the young maiden in the forest, whose limbs are charming with all-encompassing loveliness, who is beautiful in every part of her body, who stands eternally by the side of Kṛṣṇa, whose very form consists solely of love for Kṛṣṇa, and who is immersed in the essence of bliss.

I take refuge in Rādhikā in the forest— she who belongs to the Sun, who wears red garments, who is beautiful, with lovely eyes and a smiling face, who is dark-complexioned, and who grants all desires to those who are themselves dark.
Without the grace of Rādhā, the attainment of Kṛṣṇa does not occur;
therefore, one should remember Śrī Rādhikā and Kṛṣṇa in perfect union.
As it is said in the Bhaviṣyottara Purāṇa:
"O Nārada, if you have faith in love and devotion, and if you desire my grace, then become a worshiper of Rādhā with a spirit of devotion."
And so it is said in the Nāradīya: "Truth, truth, again truth, and truth indeed again and again:
without the grace of Rādhā, my grace does not exist. (GGS 190)
By the grace of Śrī Rādhikā, one may attain the company of Her friends;
and by the mercy of those friends, one may obtain the body of a woman.
In its northern petal there is a bower known as Anaṅgasukhadā;
it should be understood as having the color of lightning and being covered with various flowering trees.
In the north lies the royal grove that eternally bestows the bliss of dalliance;
there Lalitā, possessing the luster of yellow orpiment, dwells perpetually.
Clad in garments resembling peacock feathers, she is the beloved of Kṛṣṇa;
though she has experienced the state of being slighted, she is always united with Hari in love.
Abundant in the enjoyment of moon-like betel, adorned with divine ornaments, she was joined with twenty-seven days, eight months, and twenty-seven years (14-8-27). // GGS_195 //
The measure of her age is such that her father is Viśokaka,
her mother is Śāradā, and her husband is considered by the wise to be the one named Bhairava.
Having attained the state of Dāmodara in her own essential nature within the Gaurā rasa, she is indeed sharp-witted and clever;
yet Yāvatī is her home.
The definition of the *khaṇḍitā* (the neglected woman) is as follows (UN 5.85–86):
"She whose lover, having transgressed their agreement, returns in the morning marked with the signs of enjoyment from another woman— she indeed is the *khaṇḍitā*."
But this [woman] may be characterized by angry sighs, silence, and so forth. // GGS 198 //
At dawn, Śyāmalā saw the Lord of Vraja’s head smoky with [the smoke of] incense, his broad shoulders marked by the impressions of earrings,
his chest radiant with saffron transferred from her breasts, his garland withered,
and his eyes rolling and half-closed in languor.
With Rudra’s qualities in her heart, Sumukhī adopted the vow of the sages in her speech.

The characteristics of the left-handed woman (*vāma-prakharā*) are as follows (UN 6.2–5): "Because of her excellence in beauty and other qualities, she is called *adhikā* (superior); because of equality [in these], *samā* (equal); and because of inferiority, *laghu* (inferior). Thus, the beautiful-browed women of Gokula are said to be of three kinds. (GGS 200)
Each of these is further divided into three types: intense, moderate, and mild.
One who speaks boldly, is sharp-tongued, renowned for her speech, and whose words are difficult to transgress is known as *pragalbhā* (bold).
If she possesses less of these qualities, she is *mṛdvī* (gentle); if she has reached a state of equality with them, she is *madhyā* (middling).
In that regard, the "light and sharp" (laghu-prakharā) (UN 8.31)—that light and sharp [movement] is of two kinds: it may be either leftward or rightward. (GGS 203)
In this regard, the *vāmā*—

who is constantly intent on maintaining her pride and becomes angry when that pride falters, who is generally difficult to break through for the hero, and is cruel— is celebrated as the *vāmā*. (GGS 204)
In this group, Lalitā and others are proclaimed as the sharp-witted women.
An example of the *vāma* (contrary) type of *prakharā* (sharp-witted woman) is as follows (UN 8.36): "These gazelle-eyed women of Vraja, numbering more than eighty-four lakhs,
have been declared by this very companion of yours to belong to each one of you individually."
Even here on earth, she is renowned as a dear friend of great value;
how then, O rogue, do you, a reckless man, desire to seize her?
Her companions are as follows (Śrī-Kṛṣṇagaṇoddeśadīpikā 1.242):
Ratnarekhā (whose splendor is like a streak of jewels), Ratikalā, Subhadrā, and Candrarekhikā.
Sumukhī, Dhaniṣṭhā, Kalahaṃsī, and Kalāpinī.
The extraction of its mantra is as follows, according to the *Sammohana-tantra*:
"Lakṣmī, Līlā, and Lalitā; then [the seed-syllable] Ṅe, followed by the Mistress of Fire."
This eight-syllable great mantra of Lalitā bestows passion.
The mantra is as follows: Śrīṃ lāṃ lalitāyai svāhā.
The meditation upon her is as described in that very same place:
Her body emulating the luster of cow bezoar, well-attired,
wearing a garment of peacock feathers, and adorned with auspicious ornaments,
she is devoted to the enjoyment of betel by the son of the King of Vraja.
I meditate upon Lalitā, the dear friend of Śrī Rādhikā.
Indeed, on the petal of Īśāna, there is a grove named Ānanda;
it is cloud-colored, where Śrī Viśākhā, the beloved of Kṛṣṇa, resides.
For she has always attained the state of one whose husband is under her own control toward Hari;
she is fair-limbed, with a sky-like complexion, and enriched by garments, ornaments, and service.
Her age is expressed by the combination of fortnights, days, pairs of yugas, months, *manus*, and years (14-2-15).
Her father, mother, purifier, and sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) follow in sequence. (GGS 212)
Her husband, though known by the name Bāhuka, became renowned in the Kali age as Rāyarāmānanda due to his excellence in the art of love (gaura-rasa).
But this [wife] is indeed the "excessively middling" one; her household, however, lasts only for a short time.
The definition of a woman whose husband is under her own control (svādhīna-bhartṛkā) (UN 5.91): A woman whose beloved is nearby and dependent upon her is one whose husband is under her control;
she engages in sporting by water or in the forest, gathering flowers, and other such activities. (GGS 215)
An example is as follows (UN 5.92):
"Joyfully producing an incomparable sprout upon her full breasts, [the breeze] carries a pair of blue lotuses toward her two ears, which attract bees with their fragrance."
Playfully placing a soft lotus upon Rādhā’s braided hair,
the subduer of Keśin delights the untroubled Rādhā for a long time.
In this troop, Viśākhā and the others are superior and middling.
An example of the excessive and the middling [types of *udāharaṇa*] is as follows (UN 8.17):
"O Dāmodara, let this garland sent by my dear friend be offered by you; I shall place the flower here myself."
"O friend Caturikā, I should not be informed out of delusion,
since this Kṛṣṇa torments me excessively."
Her retinue is as follows (*Kṛṣṇagaṇoddeśadīpikā* 1.243):
Mālatī, Mādhavī, Candra-rekhā, and Śubhānanā; Kuñjarī, Hariṇī, Surabhi, and Capalā as well. (GGS 219)

The extraction of the mantra for this [deity] is as follows in the *Bṛhadgautamīya*: "Vāgbhava, then *sauṃ*, followed by Viśākhā in the dative case (*ṅe*-anta), and the wife of Agni (*vahni-jāyikā*)."
This eight-syllable mantra of Viśākhā bestows an increase of love.
The mantra is as follows: *aiṃ sauṃ viśākhāyai svāhā*.
The visualization (*dhyāna*) for her is as described in that very same source:
Suśīlā, whose body emulated a row of blooming campaka flowers, who wore a starry garment and shone with various ornaments,
stood before the illustrious Nandanandana, adorned with garments and finery.
I revere Viśākhā, who delights in giving and possesses great zeal.
On the eastern petal is the grove named Padmakiñjalka;
there resides the mistress Śrī Citrā, the beloved of Kṛṣṇa.
Having become an *abhisārikā* (a woman going to meet her lover) filled with passion for Hari,
she is enriched by the service of a clove garland and endowed with the complexion of saffron.
Her garment is like glass, and she is always endowed with variegated qualities;
her measurement is equal to the sky, augmented by the number of human days.
It is well known that this consists of one year of Śakra plus one month of the Ṛṣis. (GGS 225)
Her father is said to be Caturo, her mother Carccikā, and her husband is Pīṭharaka; she belongs, moreover, to the Gaura rasa.
In the midst of the fourth age, she attained the state of Govindānandā;
she is even more gentle than before, and her home is at Yāvaṭa.
The characteristics of an *abhisārikā* are as follows (UN 5.71–72):
"She who causes her lover to come to her, or who goes to him herself—whether it be by moonlight or in darkness—dressed in attire suitable for travel, is an *abhisārikā*. (GGS 228)
As if shrinking into her own limbs out of modesty, silent and with all her ornaments removed, veiled and accompanied by a single affectionate female friend, she should approach her beloved.
An example is as follows: therein,
(1) regarding a woman going to meet her lover by moonlight (*jyotsny-abhisārikā*)—
The moon spreads its orb, swollen with nectar, and its moonlight throughout Vṛndāvana;
O beautiful one, Nanda’s son gazes intently at your path, O mistress of Vraja;
you are adorned with a silken garment inlaid with moon-like sandalwood paste—
why do you not set down your pair of feet, as lovely as lotuses, upon the road?

(2) Of the woman going to meet her lover in darkness (ViM 4.22, UN 5.75): O friend, veiled by the darkness as if by ink, these meritorious women go to meet their lovers within the groves of *kadamba* trees, like the enemies of the crane (*baka*).
But around you, O Hari, these lightning-colored arrows, with shafts as bright as your own body, pierce through these thick masses of darkness, your own enemy.
In this case, various sweet substances such as madhurikā and others are used in greater quantities and with a mild consistency.

An example of excessive softness (*adhika-mṛdvī*) is as follows (UN 8.20): "O friend, though I have not even cast my gaze upon him whose crest is adorned with peacock feathers, please be gracious; do not, alas, falsely attribute fault-finding to me."
O fierce goddess, he whose crocodile-shaped earrings are swaying is suddenly spreading his playful gait nearby; what should I do in this situation?
Her retinue is as follows (*Śrī-kṛṣṇa-gaṇoddeśa-dīpikā* 1.245):
Rasālikā, Tilakinī, Śaurasenī, Sugandhikā, Vāmanī, Vāmanayanā, Nāgarī, and Nāgavallikā. (GGS 234)

The extraction of its mantra is as follows, according to the Skanda Purāṇa: "Lakṣmī" (lakṣmī), "Citrā" (citrā) ending in the fourth case, followed by the wife of Vahni (svāhā); this is the six-syllabled [mantra].
This mantra was uttered by Kṛṣṇa’s female friend named Citrikā.
The mantra is as follows: *śrīṃ citrāyai svāhā*. The visualization for her is as described in that very same source:
The one of Kashmiri complexion, endowed with manifold virtues, her face radiant with a smile, wonderful,
wearing glass-like garments, [stood] before Kṛṣṇa like a clove-flower—
I remember [this] most clearly regarding the offering of a garland.
In the southeastern petal, which has the luster of gold in a grove of full moons,
dwells Śrī Indulekhā, whose body is like yellow orpiment.
Clad in a garment shining like a pomegranate flower, the beloved of Kṛṣṇa assumes the state of a woman whose husband is away from home during the union of love.
The measurement of that [image] of the Son of Nanda, which is enriched by the service of the Eaters of Ambrosia (Amṛtāśanas),
is indeed accepted in all the scriptures.
Combined with four and a half days and ten years, two months, and two human units (14; 2;
10 1/2), she is the fierce female attendant on the left of Hari, serving him with a chowrie.
But her father, named Sāgara, was her house until she reached youth.
Her mother would be Velā, and her husband would be weak;
she is known as Vasurāmānandā, for she possesses a fair complexion. (GGS 242)
The definition of the woman whose husband is away from home (*proṣitabhartṛkā*) is as follows (UN 5.89):
"When her beloved has gone to a distant land, she becomes a *proṣitabhartṛkā*. Her [characteristics] are the recollection of her lover, dejection, emaciation, and wakefulness."
Impurity, instability, dullness, anxiety, and so forth are considered [the defects of the mind]. // GGS_243 //
An example is as follows (UN 5.90):
"The playful enemy of Madhu dwells at his own will in Mathurā, while spring spreads distress everywhere at every step."
Alas, this hostile and evil desire creates an obstacle to the undertaking of my cherished goal; what indeed shall be the refuge here? Alas! GGS 244.
The characteristics and examples of the *vāma-prakharā* have been stated;
her group (*yūtha*) is as described in the *Śrī-Kṛṣṇagaṇoddeśadīpikā* (1.247):
Tuṅgabhadrā, Citralekhā, Suraṅgī, and Raṅgavāṭikā.
Maṅgalā, Suvicitrāṅgī, Modinī, and Madanā as well.

The extraction of the mantra for this [deity] is as follows, according to the *Īśānasaṃhitā*: "Vāgbhava, Indulekhā, and the fourth is the wife of Vahni (Svāhā); this eight-syllabled mantra of Indulekhā has been proclaimed. (GGS 246)
The mantra is as follows: *aim* *indulekhāyai svāhā*.
The visualization (*dhyāna*) for her is as described in that very same source:
"Her bodily luster is equal to yellow orpiment."
Worship me as the female friend named Indulekhikā, who is adorned with garments beautiful like blooming dāṛima flowers, and who offers nectar to the face of Mukunda.
On this southern petal, there is a bower named Kāmalatā,
which bestows ultimate bliss and possesses a luster like molten gold.
"O Śrī Campakalatā, stay here; this beloved of Kṛṣṇa has become ready for the chamber, she who is the prize of love for both of us. (GGS 249)
The middle finger on the left is the color of a campaka flower; her auspicious garment has the hue of a cātaka bird.
Service to her consists of offering a garland of jewels and waving a fly-whisk.
Furthermore, the measure of age shall consist of years numbering fourteen, two months, and thirteen and a half days. (GGS 251)
Her mother is known as Vāṭikā and her father is named Ārāma;
her husband is called Caṇḍa, and she has indeed attained fame in the Kali age by the name Śivānandā because of her white complexion. (GGS 252)
The definition of the woman prepared for the night (*vāsaka-sajjā*) is as follows:
(UN 5.76–77)—She who, out of regard for her own bedchamber, prepares her body and her house when her lover is about to arrive, is called *vāsaka-sajjikā*. (GGS 253)
Her gestures consist of glancing at the path where she imagines the amorous play of love,
engaging in playful conversation with her female friends, and repeatedly sending messengers and the like.
An example is as follows (UN 5.78):
Having seen the bower for amorous play, her body with its radiant luster upon a bed of flowers, and even her own self adorned with ornaments, she has a smiling face.
Meditating again and again upon some means of union with Hari,
Rādhā’s mind became intoxicated with the madness of love.
The characteristics and examples of the *vāmaprakharā* have already been stated;
her group (*yūtha*) is as follows (from the *Kṛṣṇagaṇoddeśa*, 1.244):
"A circle of deer-eyed women, beautifully adorned with jeweled ornaments."
Caṇḍikā, Candralatikā, Kandukākṣī, and Sumandirā.
The extraction of the mantra for this [deity] is as follows in the *Garuḍa-tantra*:
"First is Campakalatā, ending in the dative case (ṅe), the beloved of Vaiśvānara;
this mantra, which bestows the love of Campakalatā, consists of eight syllables. (GGS 257)
The mantra is as follows: *campakalatāyai svāhā*.
The visualization (*dhyāna*) for this is as described in that same source:
[one should visualize her] possessing a luster equal to a garland of *campaka* flowers.
I always worship the beautiful Campaka creeper, who wears garments resembling the color of the cātaka bird, is adorned with fine ornaments, and is raised by chowries joined with jewel garlands.
In the western quarter, within a dark-colored grove called Sukhada, Śrī Raṅgadevikā, the beloved of Śrī Hari, dwells eternally. (GGS 259)
Having the luster of the filaments of a lotus, her garments resemble the *jabā* flower;
filled with a state of longing, she is always possessed of love for Śrī Kṛṣṇa. (GGS 260)
Furthermore, she who is richly adorned with sandalwood paste is one whose middle part is on the left;
moreover, her house is in the Yāvaṭa [constellation], and her stature is equal to the sky.
The human year consists of two months and four and a half days (14-2-4½).
His mother is said to be Śrī Karuṇā, and his father is Śrī Raṅgasāgara. (GGS 262)
Her husband is said to be Vakrekṣaṇa; furthermore, in the Gaurarasa [tradition], she has assumed the names Govinda, Ānanda, and Ghoṣā in the Kali age.

The definition of *utkaṇṭhitā* (longing) is as follows: (UN 5.79–80)—"When a beloved is delayed despite being innocent, she who becomes anxious is declared by those who know the [emotional] states to be *virahotkaṇṭhitā* (longing due to separation). (GGS 264)
Her outward manifestations, however, consist of heartache, trembling, conjecturing the cause, restlessness, shedding tears, describing her own condition, and so forth. (GGS 265)
An example is as follows (UN 5.81):
"O friend, was this [moon] bound by the cords of Rādhā’s sidelong glances,
or has a battle been commenced by the defiant enemies of the gods?"
Aha! O moon-faced one, on the full moon of the eighth day of the bright fortnight, even though the moon had risen in the eastern sky,
the son of the Lord of Vraja did not remember me.
The characteristics and examples of the *vāmā* and *madhyā* types have already been stated; her *yūtha* (group) is as follows (Śrī-Kṛṣṇagaṇoddeśa 1.248):
Kalakaṇṭhī, Śaśikalā, Kamalā, and Premamañjarī.
Mādhavī is sweet, the vine of desire, and beautiful as the god of love.
The extraction of the mantra for this [deity] is as follows, according to the *Kiśorī-tantra*:
"Lakṣmī, Agni, Raṅgadevī, ending with the dative suffix *ṅe*, followed by Vahni-priyā;
this eight-syllabled mantra of Raṅgadevī bestows passion and devotion. (GGS 268)
The mantra is as follows: *śrīṃ rāṃ raṅgadevyai svāhā*.
The visualization (*dhyāna*) for her is described in that very same place:
"She whose complexion is equal to the filaments of a lotus."
I worship the Goddess of the Rāsa dance-ground of the Son of Vraja’s Lord, who is adorned with garments resembling Japā flowers and attended by the service of sandalwood paste.
In the western petal there is a beautiful grove, crimson in color,
which has become renowned by the name "Bestower of the Bliss of Exalted Knowledge."
There, Tuṅgavidyā remains eternally, full of longing;
though she has been deceived, she is always endowed with love for Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
Adorned with pale ornaments and garments, and possessing the luster of moonstone, sandalwood, and abundant saffron, this woman has arisen from the southern horizon.
Medhā was born from Pauṣkarī; her husband was Bāliśa, and her home was Yāvaṭa, which abounded in the enjoyment of dance, song, and other arts. GGS 273.
Two months, two human years, and twenty-two days [are the duration]. (GGS 274)
Her age shall be such, and she shall again be of fair complexion;
indeed, in the Kali age, she shall attain the renown of being known as Vakreśvarī.
The definition of the *vipralabdha* (the deceived) heroine is as follows (UN 5.83–84):
"When, having made an appointment, the beloved of her life does not arrive due to fate,
she who is distressed within is called *vipralabdha* by the wise."
One experiences despondency, anxious reflection, exhaustion, tears, fainting, sighing, and so forth.
An example is as follows: "O friend, the moon has attained heaven, while we, though longed for by the lord of Indirā, [remain here]."
"What shall we do here? Command us respectfully and quickly!"—thus did the deer-eyed woman fall into exhaustion.
The characteristics of the *dakṣiṇā* [heroine] are as follows (UN 8.38, 42):
"When the hero is intent on pride, she does not yield; she speaks appropriately to him and is to be won over by conciliation (*sāman*). She is proclaimed to be the *dakṣiṇā*. (GGS 278)
And here, the tongue, the teeth, and so forth should be prominent and sharp on the right side.
An example is as follows (*Śrī-Gītagovinda* 9.10):

"That you are harsh toward one who is affectionate, that you are rigid when he bows down, that you harbor hatred toward one full of passion, and that you turn away from him when he looks up toward you— [all this is directed] at that beloved."
Therefore, for you who act contrary [to your nature],
sandalwood paste is poison,
the moon is the sun, snow is fire, and the joys of play are torments.
Her group [of companions] is as follows (*Śrī-kṛṣṇa-gaṇoddeśa* 1.246):
Mañjumedhā, Sumadhurā, Sumadhyā, Madhurekṣaṇā, Tanūmadhyā, Madhusyandā, Guṇacūḍā, and Varāṅgadā. (GGS 281)
The extraction of the mantra for this [deity] is as follows, according to the *Kiśorī-tantra*:
"The syllable preceded by Lakṣmī, followed by Tuṅgavidyā, and the fourth [syllable] beloved by Agni—this mantra of Tuṅgavidyā is declared to consist of eight letters. (GGS 282)
The mantra is as follows: *Śrīṃ tuṅgavidyāyai svāhā*.
The meditation (*dhyāna*) upon her is as described in that very same source:
With sandalwood paste as white as the moon, she is most graceful, possessing a splendor like the luster of auspicious saffron;
her body is adorned with ornaments set with excellent gems, and she is radiant in crimson garments.
Accompanied by a series of beautiful songs and many virtues, she is indeed celebrated by the sound of the *ḍampha* drum.
I worship Śrī Tuṅgavidyā, who dances before Hari with passionate delight.
In the petal of Vāyu is a grove of green color that grants the pleasure of spring; here, the goddess Sudevī always resides.
Having fallen into a state of being separated by a quarrel, she is difficult for even the pair of Rati and Kāma to endure;
she is as radiant as the filaments of a lotus and wears garments resembling the *japā* flower.
And that [lineage] is rich in water-service; it is considered the left-hand *prakharikā*, consisting of four years—two months and two days added to the Vedic [four] days. (GGS 286)
Her age and her dwelling place are as follows:
her mother is said to be Karuṇā, and her father is Raṅgasāgara. GGS 287.
She was married by her younger brother Vakrekṣaṇa;
she obtained the name Śrīvāsudevaghoṣā, yet she remained immersed in the mellows of the fair-complexioned Lord (Gaurarasa).
The definition of the *kalahāntaritā* (the woman separated by a quarrel) is as follows (UN 5.87):
She who, having angrily repulsed her beloved when he fell at her feet in front of her friends, later feels remorse— she is indeed the *kalahāntaritā*.
Her lamentations, feverish distress, exhaustion, sighs, and so forth [arise from this].
An example is as follows (UN 5.88):
"Garlands were cast far away by Keśiripu himself,
yet his sweet words were not uttered even within the vicinity of his ears."
I did not notice him as he prostrated himself, his crest-lock rolling upon the ground;
my mind was elsewhere, and because of that, it is bursting within me like a flower extracted from a *puṭapāka* oven.
The characteristics and examples of the left-hand sharp [type] have already been stated;
her group is as follows (Śrī-Kṛṣṇagaṇoddeśadīpikā 1.249): Kāverī, Cārukavarī, Sukeśī, and Mañjukeśikā.
Hārahīrā, Hārakaṇṭhī, Hāravallī, and Manoharā.
The extraction of her mantra is as follows, according to the *Rudrayāmala*: "Two [syllables] of Vāgbhava, Ramā, followed by *ṅe*, then Sudevī and Dahana-priyā.
This eight-syllabled mantra of Sudevī has been declared; it bestows loving devotion. (GGS 292)
The mantra is as follows: *aiṃ sauṃ śrīṃ sudevyai svāhā*.
The visualization (*dhyāna*) for her is as described in that same source:
"She whose luster is equal to the filaments of a lotus, who is of excellent character..."
I worship the noble goddess Sudevi, who wears red garments, whose face shines with a beautiful smile,
who is richly engaged in pouring water before the illustrious Nandanandana,
and who is adorned with a series of excellent ornaments.
To the north of the grove of Lalitā, there is a grove named Rūpollāsa;
there, the most beautiful Rūpamañjarī always resides.
Sundarī Rūpamañjarī was the chief of her dear jesting companions;
the beauty of her limbs was like yellow orpiment, and she was fond of garments adorned with peacock feathers.
At thirteen and a half years of age, she has resorted to the state of being both left-handed and central;
the wise call her Raṅgaṇamālikā. (GGS 296)
In a single day, this younger sister of Lavaṅgamañjarī attained the status of Rūpagosvāmī within the fair-complexioned community during the Kali age.
The extraction of her mantra is as follows in the *Kiśorī-tantra*:
"Rūpamañjarī, joined with the Śrī-bīja and ending in the vocative case (ṅe), is declared to be this eight-syllabled mantra of Rūpamañjarī. (GGS 298)
The mantra is as follows: *śrīṃ rūpamañjaryai svāhā*.
The meditation upon her is as described in that very same source: "Her own bodily luster surpasses that of yellow pigment (*gorocanā*)."
I worship Mañjarikā, known as Rūpā, the handmaid at the lotus feet of Śrī Rādhikā, who wears fine garments with the luster of a peacock’s tail feathers. GGS 299.
To the south of the Indulekhā grove lies the grove known as Ratyambuja;
there alone always resides the beautiful Rati-mañjarī.
This Tārāvalī, whose body has a luster like lightning and who wears silken garments, is known as the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā);
they call her Mṛdvīkā and Tulasī.
Her age is thirteen years and two months;
she has attained the name Śrī Raghunātha within the Gaura-rasa in the Kali age. (GGS 302)
The extraction of the mantra for this [deity] is as follows in the *Kiśorī-tantra*:
"Fire (RA) joined with Nāda (the bindu) and Bindu (the anusvāra), endowed with the face and the circle;
ending with SVĀHĀ, the Mañjarī [mantra], ending with ṄE, is the mantra of Ratimañjarikā. (GGS 303)
The mantra is as follows: *rāṃ rati-mañjaryai svāhā*.
Her visualization (*dhyāna*) is as described in that same [text]:
"Wearing a pair of garments with the hue of a swarm of bees..."
I worship that beautiful Ratimañjarī, whose own body’s luster is like lightning, who dwells in the presence of Śrī Rādhikā.
In the eastern part of the grove of lofty learning,
there exists a grove named Lavaṅgasukhada, which is most enchanting to those of beautiful vision.
There, Lavaṅgamañjarī always remains with joy;
she is indeed superior to Rūpamañjarī by a single day.
Possessing a splendor like rising lightning, draped in a garment of starry clusters, the southern grape is considered to eternally bestow the bliss of Śrī Kṛṣṇa. (GGS 307)
In age, he was one day and thirteen and a half years old;
this one named Śrī Sanātana became renowned in the Kali age for his devotion to the mellows of the fair-complexioned Lord. (GGS 308)
The extraction of the mantra for this [deity] is as follows in the *Kiśorī-tantra*:
"Joined with the two syllables of Śrī and Līlā, ending in the dative case (ṅe), is Lavaṅgamañjarī."
Svāhā! This ten-syllable mantra is for the clove bud. // GGS_309 //
The mantra is as follows: *Śrīṃ lāṃ lavaṅga-mañjaryai svāhā*.
The visualization (*dhyāna*) for this is as described in that very same source:
"She whose splendor puts to shame the radiance of lightning."
I worship that Lavanga-mañjarī, who delights the son of the King of Vraja and whose garments are adorned by beautiful rows of stars.
To the west of Citrakuñja there is a grove named Rasānandaprada;
there, Rasamañjarī always dwells.
She is celebrated as the perfect life-giver to Śrī Rūpamañjarī;
clad in silken garments like the wings of a swan, she possesses the luster of a blossoming campaka flower.
Generally equal to a cluster of cloves in her wealth of virtues, she who has taken refuge in Śrī Rūpamañjarī has attained extreme endearment. (GGS 313)
This clever woman, who has acquired skill in diplomacy through her reconciliation efforts,
is considered a "Southern Grapes" (dakṣiṇā mṛdvikā), being thirteen autumns of age. (13) GGS 314.
In the Kali age, she has attained the status of Bhaṭṭa, joined with the name Raghunātha.
The extraction of the mantra for this [goddess] is as follows, according to the *Kiśorī-tantra*:
"Joined with the face and the circle, endowed with fire, sound, and the bindu, ending with *svāhā* and the dative case—this is indeed the *Rasa-mañjarī* mantra. (GGS 316)
The mantra is as follows: *rāṃ rasa-mañjaryai svāhā*.
The visualization (*dhyāna*) for her is as described in that very same source:
"Clad in a garment as beautiful as the wings of a swan..."
I worship Rasa-mañjarī, who possesses the luster of a full-blown campaka flower, who is endowed with the perfection of beautiful form and virtues, and who is ever-present.
In the northeast, from the grove of Campaka creepers, there is a beautiful grove named Guṇānandaprada; therein dwells Guṇamañjarī.
She who desires the pleasure of the *rūpamañjarikā* is thus described;
she possesses the luster of a mass of lightning, with a garment like a row of hibiscus flowers.
In three days, this Tulasi becomes the youngest [sister] of Him;
she speaks with sharp eloquence, having taken refuge in the courtesy of Śrī Kṛṣṇa’s fragrance.
Her age is stated to be thirteen years plus one month, together with twenty-seven days. (GGS 3.21)
In the Kali age, he shall be renowned by the name Gopālabhaṭṭa within the Gaurāṅga rasa.

The mantra is as follows: *gāṃ guṇamañjaryai svāhā*.
The visualization (*dhyāna*) for her is as described in that same source:
"She is richly adorned with silken garments resembling the color of the *jaba* flower, and her body possesses a luster like a streak of lightning."
I worship Guṇamañjarī, who has made her expectation [of reward] dependent upon Kṛṣṇāmoda.
In the region to the north of Kuñjaka, belonging to Sudevi, there is one named Līlānandaprada;
there indeed always resides Mañjulālī Sumañjarī.
With her wealth of virtues, she is like a friend to the *rūpamañjarikā* plant;
she wears a garment of sapphire-blue stripes and possesses a complexion like molten gold.
Līlāmañjarī by name occupies the position of her left middle finger;
she is seventeen years of age, being joined with seven fortnights. (GGS 327)
In the Kali age, they attained the status of Gosvāmins as Lords of the World within the Gaura-rasa.
The extraction of the mantra for this [goddess] is as follows, according to the *Kiśorī-tantra*:
"Mañjulālī joined with Lakṣmī, followed by Mañjarī and the wife of Vahni (Svāhā), ending in the dative case—this ten-syllable mantra is indeed declared. (GGS 329)
The mantra is as follows: *Śrīṃ mañjulālī-mañjaryai svāhā*.
The visualization (*dhyāna*) for this is as described in that same source:
"She who possesses the luster of limbs like molten gold, who is enchanting..."
I constantly worship that Mañjulālī, who wears crimson garments, is richly adorned with beautiful ornaments, and is a servant at the lotus feet of Śrī Rādhikā.
To the southeast of Vaiśākha-kuñja there is a most enchanting grove that bestows the joy of amorous play; by name it is called Vilāsa-mañjarī, and there dwells [the goddess] Vilāsa-mañjarī.
Vilāsamañjarī, having entered into friendship with Rūpamañjarī,
made the divine golden ketaka flower appear similar to herself by means of her own radiance.
This left hand, like a bee and a fine silk garment, has attained softness;
in four days, it shall become the youngest finger of the cluster of nectar. (GGS 333)
In the Kali age, he attained the status of Jīva Gosvāmī within the Gaurarasa tradition.
The extraction of the mantra for this [deity] is as follows, according to the *Kiśorī-tantra*: "Śrī, Pracetas, Nāda, Bindu, and the syllables Āsya-vṛtta-gā;
followed by Vilāsa-mañjarī, ending with *ṅe*, and concluding with *svāhā*—this is declared to be the mantra. (GGS 335)
The mantra is as follows: *Śrīṃ vāṃ vilāsa-mañjaryai svāhā*.
The visualization (*dhyāna*) for her is as described in that same source: "Her body surpasses the golden *ketaka* flower..."
I worship Suvilāsa-mañjarī, whose garments possess a luster like that of a censured bee,
and who serves the lotus-feet of Kṛṣṇa.
To the southwest, from the grove of Śrīraṅgadevī, there is a western grove named Kaustūryānandada; there dwells Kaustūrīmañjarī.
Her garment is like glass, she possesses the luster of limbs of pure gold,
she is thirty years of age, and this beautiful woman has attained softness.
In the Kali age, he attained the name Śrī-Kṛṣṇa-Kavirāja within the aesthetic relish of the fair-complexioned Lord (Gaurarasa).
The extraction of the mantra for this [deity] is as follows in the *Kiśorī-tantra*:
"Joined with the seed-syllable *Śrī*, ending in *Ṅe*, [followed by] *Kaustūrī-mañjarī* and ending in *Svāhā*—this is declared to be the nine-syllabled mantra. (GGS 340)
The mantra is as follows: *śrīṃ kastūrī-mañjaryai svāhā*.
The visualization (*dhyāna*) for this is as stated in that very same source:
"She whose body has the luster of a pure golden lotus..."
I worship Kaustūrī-mañjarikā, who dwells near Śrī Rādhikā, wearing garments as beautiful and charming as the luster of glass.

Then one should meditate upon the two Lords of Vṛndāvana, situated in the midst of the filaments of a lotus, possessing the beauty of ten million Cupids, and surrounded by their dear female companions.

The practitioner, endowed with the means of accomplishment, should visualize [the two deities] as being joined with the aforementioned dress, age, and form, exceedingly beautiful, and possessing perfected bodies.

Therein, first one should remember one's own respective spiritual masters (gurus) and others in the form of flower-clusters (mañjarī), according to their own specific traditions, following the sequence of the venerable guru and the supreme guru; thereafter, one should meditate upon Śrī Rādhikā, and then upon Śrī Nandanandana.
Now, the extraction of the mantra for the Couple (Yugala-mantra) is as follows, according to the Sanat-kumāra-saṃhitā:
One should recite "gopījana-vallabha" and "caraṇau" in sequence, followed by "śaraṇaṃ prapadye"; these are the two subsequent words. (GGS 344)
The mantra consisting of three words is declared to have sixteen syllables;
having uttered "namo gopījana," one should then say "vallabhābhyām. The mantra consisting of two words is indeed said to have ten syllables. (GGS 345)
The mantra is as follows: *gāṃ gopījana-vallabha-caraṇān śaraṇaṃ prapadye, namo gopījana-vallabhābhyām*.
The meditation upon this is as described in that very same place:
Now, O best of the twice-born, I shall explain the meditation upon this mantra:
[one should visualize the deity] clad in yellow garments, dark as a rain cloud, two-armed, and wearing a forest garland.
The Lord, whose hair is adorned with peacock feathers, whose face resembles ten million moons,
whose eyes are rolling, and who wears karṇikāra flowers as ear-ornaments.
Then, with sandalwood paste on both sides and a drop of saffron in the center,
a variegated tilaka in the shape of a mandala was worn upon the forehead.
He was resplendent with two earrings resembling the rising sun,
and his cheeks shone like mirrors upon which drops of perspiration glistened.
Upon the face of his beloved, her brow was raised by the playful movement of the outer corner of her eye, and her prominent,
well-formed nose shone with a pearl set in its upper part.
With lips like a ripe bimba fruit shining with the moonlight of her teeth,
and hands resplendent with armlets, bracelets, and rings set with fine jewels.
He holds a flute in his left hand and likewise a lotus in his right;
his waist is radiant with a girdle-string, and his feet shine with anklets.
[He saw] the fickle-eyed one, restless with the intense passion of amorous play,
laughing together with his beloved and repeatedly making her laugh.
Thus, one should meditate upon Kṛṣṇa seated with his beloved upon a jeweled lion-throne at the foot of the wish-fulfilling tree in the forest of Vṛndāvana.
Then one should remember Rādhikā, standing at his left side,
wearing beautiful blue garments and possessing a radiance like molten gold.
Her limbs were covered by the hem of her garment; her lotus-like face was smiling;
with her flickering eyes like those of a female cakora bird, she cast glances toward the face of her beloved.
And with her thumb and forefinger, she is offering to the lotus-face of her own beloved a betel vine leaf combined with areca nut powder.
Her beautiful, full, and elevated breasts gleam with a pearl necklace;
she has a slender waist and broad hips, adorned with a network of tinkling bells.
She wears jeweled earrings and anklets, and jeweled rings upon her toes;
her limbs are charming with the essence of loveliness, and she is beautiful in every part of her body.
O best of Brahmins, she should be immersed in the essence of bliss, serene, and in the bloom of youth; her female companions, possessing similar age and qualities,
should be intent on serving her with fly-whisks, fans, and other such attendances.
And yet—
seated upon the lion-throne in a magnificent jeweled palace beneath a wish-fulfilling tree in the divine forest of Vṛndāvana;
I remember the illustrious Śrī Rādhā and Śrīla Govinda-deva, being served by their most beloved companions.
In this manner, the practitioner, having perfected his body through the sequence of practice,
should meditate upon the two Lords of Vraja situated on the filaments of the lotus along with their respective instruments.
